claims.text: The particles are initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Chemical complexity governs the premelting and melting behavior of these nanoparticles.
Nanoscale phase-transition behavior governs the premelting and melting response.
Variation among nanoparticle configurations contributes to their premelting and melting behavior.
Combining in situ characterization with simulations can provide mechanistic understanding of nanoparticle behavior.
The proposed simulations are atomistic simulations suitable for validating models of premelting and melting.
The interplay of chemical complexity, nanoscale phase-transition behavior, and varied configurations produces unique premelting and melting behavior.
The high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit premelting and melting behavior that differs significantly from single-metal nanoparticles.
The high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit premelting and melting behavior that differs significantly from bimetallic nanoparticles.
Any difference from single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles is caused by increased chemical complexity and configuration diversity.
The hypothesis applies only within a specific composition and particle-size range.
The hypothesis may not generalize to other nanoparticle or material systems.
The exact interplay among chemical complexity, phase-transition behavior, and configuration is not yet understood.
Premelting and melting temperatures, phase-transition behavior, composition, and configuration will be measured in a controlled comparison.
Similarity between the high-entropy-alloy and baseline nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
